questions.stem: A can completely do a piece of work in exactly 15 days, while B can do the exact same work in 10 days. If they work together, in how many days will they complete the work?
questions.explanation: A's 1 day's work = 1/15. B's 1 day's work = 1/10. Together, their 1 day's work = (1/15) + (1/10) = 2/30 + 3/30 = 5/30 = 1/6. Therefore, working together, they will finish the entire work in exactly 6 days.

questions.stem: A and B working together can complete a specific task in exactly 4 days. If A alone can complete the same task in exactly 12 days, how many days would B alone take to complete the task?
questions.explanation: (A + B)'s 1 day's work = 1/4. A's 1 day's work = 1/12. B's 1 day's work = (1/4) - (1/12) = 3/12 - 1/12 = 2/12 = 1/6. Therefore, B alone can complete the work in exactly 6 days.

questions.stem: A is twice as good a workman as B, and together they can finish a piece of work in exactly 14 days. In how many days can A alone finish the exact same work?
questions.explanation: Let B's efficiency be 1 unit/day, so A's efficiency is 2 units/day. Their combined efficiency is 3 units/day. Since they finish the work in 14 days, total work = 14 × 3 = 42 units. Time taken by A alone = Total work ÷ A's efficiency = 42 ÷ 2 = 21 days.

questions.stem: A can do a piece of work in exactly 24 days and B can do it in 30 days. They work together for 5 days, and then A leaves the job. How many days will B take to strictly finish the remaining work?
questions.explanation: Let total work = LCM(24, 30) = 120 units. A's efficiency = 120/24 = 5 units/day. B's efficiency = 120/30 = 4 units/day. Together, they do 9 units/day. Work done in 5 days = 9 × 5 = 45 units. Remaining work = 120 - 45 = 75 units. Time taken by B to finish remaining work = 75 ÷ 4 = 18.75 days, which is 18 and 3/4 days.

questions.stem: A, B, and C can complete a piece of work in 24, 6, and 12 days respectively. If they all work together, in how many days will they completely finish the same work?
questions.explanation: Let total work = LCM(24, 6, 12) = 24 units. A's efficiency = 1 unit/day; B's efficiency = 4 units/day; C's efficiency = 2 units/day. Total efficiency = 1 + 4 + 2 = 7 units/day. Total time taken by all three = Total work ÷ Total efficiency = 24 ÷ 7 = 3 and 3/7 days.

questions.stem: A and B can do a piece of work in exactly 12 days, B and C in 15 days, and C and A in exactly 20 days. If A, B, and C work together, how many days will B alone take to completely finish the work?
questions.explanation: Let the 1 day's work of A, B, and C be a, b, and c. We have: (a+b)=1/12, (b+c)=1/15, (c+a)=1/20. Adding all three gives 2(a+b+c) = 1/12 + 1/15 + 1/20 = 5/60 + 4/60 + 3/60 = 12/60 = 1/5. So, (a+b+c) = 1/10. We need B alone, which is 'b'. b = (a+b+c) - (c+a) = 1/10 - 1/20 = 2/20 - 1/20 = 1/20. Therefore, B alone can do the work in 20 days.

questions.stem: A and B together can do a piece of work in exactly 30 days. They worked together for 20 days, and then B unexpectedly left. After another 20 days, A successfully finished the remaining work. In how many days can A alone finish the entire whole work?
questions.explanation: Together, A and B do 1/30 of the work per day. In 20 days, they complete 20 × (1/30) = 2/3 of the work. The remaining work is 1 - 2/3 = 1/3. A completes this remaining 1/3 of the work in exactly 20 days. Therefore, to complete the whole work (1 full unit), A alone would take 20 × 3 = 60 days.
